spec.cap: route recovers the keys — but only because they are words typed in the box, so its outlets are still bare nubs counted left to right (the third is the unmatched rest). And the cold inlets must be loaded before the hot one: a keyword arriving after the positional argument is simply late.

There is no pair of ports to reorder. Both arguments are rows in the node's side panel, and the single wire on the wall carries items, not arguments — reordering the keywords changes the form, never the canvas.

Only the positional argument is a cable at all — it lands on nub 0 of the bar's TOP edge and leaves from the bottom. force= and approach= are real keywords typed into the parameter pane beside the canvas and drawn nowhere. Invoke Compiled Block is the one exception: its nubs match by Input Name, still typed off-canvas.

The one bucket where **cfg is free: there was never a statically-known port list to lose. The keys ride inside msg and the subflow reads whichever it finds at run time — this board is identical whether cfg holds two keys or twenty.

The star has to become a NUMBER before it can become a wall: In1/In2/In3 are three separate capsules and 'Number of inputs: 3' is typed into the Mux dialog, invisible until you open it. A fourth pose is a dialog edit, not a cable — and the parent rectangle then grows a fourth numbered stub.

The count is written as text: `0. 0. 0.` is the whole of the star, and the inlet wall is just a readout of it. Only one inlet is hot, so b and c merely sit in storage until a arrives — splat order is the patch's geometry, not its cords.

The star is literally a number in that same dialog: -1 means whatever is left. How wide that second wire actually is appears nowhere unless signal-dimension display is switched on; LabVIEW's Array Subset and Max's `zl slice 1` fork the same way.

Grasshopper has no definition/call split, so `def merge(*poses)` is just a capsule — and the star is three noodles dropped onto the SAME P grip. Every one of those noodles carries a single item, so every one stays a thin single line: the grip keeps a source LIST (IGH_Param 'knows how to collect and interweave data from multiple sources'), but that list exists only inside the grip and is drawn nowhere. Three cables converging on one dot is the entire mark, and which of them is poses[0] is never printed.

Three cables on one dot — the ellipsis socket SHAPE is the only mark that says many, and it exists on built-ins like Join Geometry but never on a group's own wall. So the splat can be drawn, but only outside the callee: drag a noodle up or down and poses[0] silently changes.

Split List at i=1 is the whole of `first, *rest` — except A comes back as a one-item LIST, so a second capsule is what finally produces Python's scalar. Blender forks the same way with Separate Geometry's Selection / Inverted pair.

nodes.tag: at most one input nub, ever

spec.cap: Neither other bucket's mark is available here: no count field to grow ports from, and no grip that COLLECTS. A second cable CAN land on that one untyped nub — it just does not gather: the two messages arrive one after the other and the callee sees two runs, never a list of two. So the arity can only ride as text inside msg.payload, and this wall is identical for one pose or twenty.

merge(poses) and merge(*poses) are the same picture; only the little '3 items' label moves. Whether the callee sees three calls or one list is a side-panel toggle the canvas cannot show — and Node-RED prints not even the label.

The star is a clock, not a shape: split re-emits one message per detection on the same nub, so first and rest never coexist on the canvas — only msg.parts.index tells them apart, and that rides inside the payload.

The await IS the Completed pin — a second white exec output that fires later, which is why the work sits in an Event Graph and not a Function. Unity stamps the same idea as a coroutine badge on the header; Simulink as a dot-dashed E3() on the top edge.
There is no gather node: Sequence fires both and the join is hand-built from a counter and a Branch. The two poses never meet on one wire, so Python's tuple has no drawing at all.

Nothing on this canvas is a Task object. create_task is Then 0 handing control straight back, and await task is wherever the Completed pin lands — the graph names where execution resumes, never what is pending.

Both awaits vanish — every wire here is already an asynchronous delivery, so an awaited call is just a tile. Node-RED and Max draw the identical chain; a Wait / Delay / deferlow box appears only when you want a pause.

The fork looks like concurrency and is not: n8n runs the upper branch to completion first, ordered by canvas height. Merge only makes the tuple — Node-RED spells that `join`, and neither tool has a gather.

Max has no future object: `t b b` fixes the order — right outlet first, so classify runs now — and `deferlow` is the only box on the patch that means later. Awaiting the task is simply where its cord eventually lands.
There is no await mark because the wire already is one — a subVI fires the instant its inputs arrive. The dash-hatched error wire is what you invent when two calls must be ordered but share no data.
The gather is the gap: nothing wires the two branches to each other, and that missing wire IS the claim that they run at once. Bundle makes the tuple, not the concurrency.

The one place the future becomes a visible object: the strictly-typed refnum running from Start to Wait On Asynchronous Call IS the task. Classify.vi sits beside it touching none of it — which is exactly what makes it concurrent.
Identical to the synchronous drawing, node for node. Flyde's only cue lives at runtime — the cord holds green while the promise is unresolved; Blender, Houdini and Grasshopper show nothing even then.

A fork here says nothing about concurrency: Blender pulls both branches backwards from Group Output and never draws the order. Houdini's whole concurrency control is a Multithread when Compiled checkbox in the parameter pane.

nodes.t: A stored task has no drawing in any of these four. Grasshopper re-solves the entire document synchronously, so no grip can hold a pending value; Blender and Houdini have no time axis inside a geometry network at all; and Flyde's promise never leaves the node that made it. `task = create_task(...)` therefore draws the same fork as any other branch, and `await task` is not a node — the classify branch simply sits beside it, indistinguishable.

spec.cap: The refusal has a hard edge here: these tools can draw a fork, but they cannot put a not-yet-arrived value on a wire, so example 3 is unrepresentable rather than merely unmarked.

nodes.t: Undrawable. Both boards re-solve from scratch on every change, so no capsule can hold a value a later capsule reads. self.last has to become a wire from update into predict — which makes them one chain, not two methods. In Flyde it can only hide inside a Code Node's body.

The aliasing Python spells out is the default state here — two names for one value is just ordinary fan-out off one grip, drawn no differently.

strict=True costs no node, no wire and no canvas space — a checkbox sitting on the Data Input port's own row, invisible to anyone tracing the white control wire.

None is drawn exactly as 2.0 would be — an object pin's default box simply reads None — so the board shows a default value and can never show an absent argument. Blender has no null at all and cannot reach this example.
LabVIEW is the one tool here where the blank left wall really is the mark — a Constant has an output stub and no input at all — and its orange border, not any text, is what says DBL.

Both message boxes carry an inlet on their own top edge — a `set` message rewrites the text — so 'no input' is never Max's mark; and Max has no True, so the flag is a box holding 1 that must reach the cold inlet BEFORE the path hits the hot one, an ordering the cords never draw.
Simulink has no None, so the pill must carry a stand-in number — NaN, -1, 0 — and the board cannot tell you which of them means 'absent' rather than 'measured'.
Nothing on the canvas changed when 2.0 was set — the bar, its nubs and its one grey wire look identical at 1.0 — so the board carries routing and the side panel carries the arithmetic.

Both nested calls, the separator and the template are one VEX line in a field; the grey wire says only that geometry cooks downward — the fan-in the f-string really is never reaches the board.

The literal text BETWEEN the braces has to become nodes too, and :.2f is the Decimals field on Value to String. Four wires land on one multi-input socket, so the sentence is stored as the drag order of those wires — nothing else records it.

Simulink: there is no object and no assignment — the whole `+= 1` is the visible closed ring, and the 1/z is the only thing keeping it from being an algebraic loop.

nodes.t: No mark exists. Two capsules sharing no wire solve in an order the canvas never states, and neither touches Rhino until an explicit Bake — so gripper.open() before arm.move_to() is unsayable here.

spec.cap: The one example this vocabulary cannot draw: with no sink and no ordering edge, an effect-only call has nowhere to land.
The join needs no node — two white exec wires land on the Return Node's ONE exec input; it is the exec OUTPUT pin that may take only a single wire.
There is no elif: the second Branch hangs off the first's False pin, so the board staircases down-right one step per arm and the three arms are never siblings.
The implicit else is a real, drawn wire: False is dragged past the arm onto the same downstream exec input — leave that pin hollow and execution silently stops instead of falling through.
The else arm is not off-screen, it is behind this one — the ▾ is the only way to see it, and LabVIEW refuses to run until EVERY hidden case has wired that one output tunnel.
elif is nesting, not a third case: only the 'B' arm is on screen, 'A' is one ▾ click away and 'C' is two — the flat Python chain becomes a depth gradient.
The do-nothing arm still costs a wire: in the unseen True case the left tunnel must be dragged straight across to the right one, or the output tunnel goes hollow and the VI breaks.
The dot-dashed line enters the subsystem's TOP edge at an Action Port and carries no value — only 'run now'; the join is a real Merge block, legal only because the two writers are mutually exclusive.
elif is a third line of text on the SAME If block, so the chain stays flat — and u1 and u2 are both computed every time step regardless; the If block only licenses which subsystem may run.

Nothing here is the implicit else: Merge's Initial output feeds only the FIRST time step, and after that the signal holds its last value — Python's assignment has to be drawn as a second arm, or the whole thing collapses to one Switch block.
Both wires stay drawn and neither is greyed — only the one that actually carried items turns green after a run; Flyde spells the same card 'Conditional' with pins named true and false.
elif flattens to three nubs read top-down with 'otherwise' last — but 'stop after first match' is a checkbox in the edit dialog, so unchecked, ALL matching rules fire and grade is set three times.
Max patches the same mechanism downward: select's rightmost outlet is the no-match case, and the implicit else is simply that outlet left unpatched — the cord that did not fire is still drawn, unlit.
The choice happens at the END, not the start: both arms are upstream siblings, the Switch collapses them to ONE output dot, and which arm actually ran is nowhere on the canvas.

The entire elif chain is a ternary typed into Select Input, off-canvas in the Parameter Editor — the board shows three arms that all exist and one nub that picks; wires pull, so the unchosen arms never cook and nothing on the bar says which.

No implicit else and no skipped work — Estimate solves on every recompute even when its wire is not the one chosen, because Dispatch and Stream Filter split the DATA, never the execution; only the Gate index decides what emerges.

The whole second Python clause is then one capsule — which in practice often is not even drawn, collapsing to a tiny flatten icon on the downstream grip. n8n calls it Split Out; Blender has no list-flatten node at all.

The array crosses the wall whole and ONE element appears inside — the [ ] brackets on the tunnel are the entire iteration, and the loop's count N and iteration i terminals are left unwired. Simulink's For Each Subsystem is the same rectangle and, unlike For Iterator, emits no index stub to wire anything to.

The predicate is declared ON THE WALL — a ? tunnel with a Boolean stub under it — so the output array just comes out shorter and no node inside ever learns it was filtered. The test is one glyph: Not Equal To 0? is its own primitive with a single input, not the two-input Not Equal?. Simulink cannot do this at all — its signals are fixed-size, so every element computes and a Switch picks a held value.

Two Python clauses, ONE region: the inner loop vanishes into the tunnel's Concatenating mode, which appends each bin's list instead of stacking them into a zero-padded 2-D array. Simulink has no such mode, so a ragged flatten has no Simulink drawing.

The per-element loop has NO mark on the canvas whatsoever: it is a Run Over dropdown in the parameter pane, and the expression is one line of VEX typed off-screen. The tag under the bar is drawn here for the reader — in Houdini you cannot see it from the network view at all.

Map and filter are the SAME box — two lines in one parameter field. This board is pixel-identical to the unfiltered one before it: the only difference is characters nobody can see from the network view.

The double loop is one stock bar with no expression at all — a container's contents ARE its geometry, so flattening is a type change, not an iteration. Nothing is typed anywhere on this board, and nothing is drawn either.

Unlike Houdini, Max's loop is characters you CAN read: `vexpr`'s own title text is the comprehension, list into one inlet, mapped list out of one outlet, no iteration drawn. The catch is in that same text — `vexpr` speaks only arithmetic, so a real `estimate` abstraction splits this single box into the chain on the next board.

The predicate is still legible text, but the single box is gone: `vexpr` cannot drop an element, so the list is torn into items by `zl iter` and reassembled by `zl group` — which must be told how many to wait for, and cannot be, because the count is only known once the run is over. This is the Flyde/Node-RED row spelled in Max, and the same failure it hits.

A Max list cannot contain a list, so the outer collection is not a list at all — it is a `coll`, and the outer loop is `uzi` machine-gunning indices at it. Flattening is then free because nothing was ever nested. Nothing is typed in a box on this board: for two clauses Max leaves its own bucket entirely.

No frame, and no output wire: the comprehension's result exists only as the Poses VARIABLE feeding Add's Array pin, and the white Loop Body pin — not any cable — is what says 'once per element'. Unity draws the identical shape with a For Each Loop's Body arrow and a Set Variable.

Same Add node as the first board, Array pin and all, now fed by a Good variable — only the exec wire reaching it has changed. There is no filter node: the predicate becomes a GREY Branch on the exec wire (grey is Blueprint's flow-control title bar; purple is reserved for function entry/return), and an element is dropped by leaving the False pin wired to nothing. Estimate is PURE — no exec pin — so a dropped element never computes at all.

Two clauses become two loop NODES chained on the white wire — the outer Loop Body fires the inner ForEachLoop, and only the innermost body reaches the Add whose Array pin holds the Items variable. Nothing encloses anything, so nesting depth is read off the exec chain alone.

Three cards on one grey wire: 'item' fires once per element, and Collect is told how many to wait for by wiring the loop's own length pin into it — the count pin only appears because that count was made dynamic. Node-RED draws the identical row as two pale-yellow Split / Join nodes bracketing the body.

The filter is a fourth card whose 'false' pin is left dangling — that dangle IS the drop. Note what it costs, and that you can SEE the cost: the count pin on Collect is gone, because nobody knows the length until the run is over, so the card falls back to one of its other two strategies — close after a time, or close when a trigger arrives.

Two clauses, two Loop List cards in a row — and only ONE Collect at the end, which is exactly why flattening is free here: the inner items were never grouped, so there is nothing to un-nest. It pays the same price as the filtered board: neither loop's length is the total, so Collect closes on time, not on a count.

Two resources, two hand-built lifetimes: opening is a message box you bang, and the release is a free-floating closebang that fires when the PATCHER closes - not when the work ends, and never on failure.

Three nodes on one white exec wire; the grey comment box is the ONLY thing pairing acquire with release and it carries no semantics - if Move To fails the wire stops there and the lock is never released.

LabVIEW's one frame whose RIGHT border node always runs - a genuine guaranteed exit. But what it guarantees is that the element goes back into the cluster; a lock carries no value, so there is nothing to hand the border nodes.

One Python statement becomes two NESTED nodes. Each Finally closes its own file, but only the nesting says which runs first - and nothing on the canvas marks the two as one scope.

gain can never arrive as a second cable into the body — the single nub is already taken by the item stream, so the only way in is to hide it inside msg, set once upstream of `split`.
The outlets carry no labels: each is typed by the argument sitting above it in the text, and which member it carries is purely its position — the names exist only in the two v boxes at the bottom.

Its rows print the field NAMES and each leaves in that field's own wire colour, so cluster order stops mattering — Blender's Separate Bundle and Simulink's Bus Selector (<pose>, <quality>) read the same; Flyde's Spread List is the positional cousin, item1…itemN.

The splitter has nothing to do here: nothing is named, so the whole statement is two beziers dragged to cross the grips — and re-dragging a grip replaces its source in place, leaving no record the board ever ran the other way.

No Break node was added — the struct pin itself split and its members indented on the call node's wall; the two names then cost two SET nodes strung along the white wire, so one Python line is three nodes and an order.

Not one wire runs between the three calls. The frame walls ARE the order, and the constant feeding Move To lives inside its own frame because that is the only place it is allowed to matter.

The frames share a wall, so nothing can reach frame 1 directly: `frame` tunnels INTO frame 0, straight across it, and out the far side just to get to Estimate.vi. Validate.vi's `ok` stub dangles unread — the wall is what orders it, and the plumbing is what that costs.

`pose` is computed in frame 1 and read outside the structure, so it leaves frame 1's right wall and then has to cross frame 2 as well — two more tunnels for a value frame 2 never touches. The film strip routes the data, not just the order.

One grey wire kind, handed along in series. Nothing says the arm needs anything from the gripper — and `target` is invisible too, riding inside msg.payload, so a wire carrying a value and a wire carrying only a turn are drawn identically.

The chain runs top to bottom and Houdini only cooks what someone downstream asks for, so a discarded call must still be wired somewhere. With Copy Input off NULL1 emits empty geometry — its wire into merge1 is drawn exactly like estimate's and carries nothing.

Blender has no second wire to reach for, so the order is converted into data: one Geometry noodle threaded through all three nodes in the order you want them run. Nothing marks which link is a real dependency and which is only a leash.

The dash-hatched olive wire is a real value — an error cluster nobody in this diagram reads — threaded through all three VIs solely to order them. Its pattern is unlike any other wire on the board, which is exactly why LabVIEW authors reach for it instead of a Sequence Structure.

Validate.vi's real result is never wired anywhere. The only thing joining the two VIs is the olive error cluster running into a pin literally named `error in` — order carried by a wire whose type and pin name both announce they are not the payload.

The trigger pin is an ordinary input whose text label is replaced by a lightning bolt: whatever lands on it is discarded, only its arrival matters. It stays hidden until you right-click 'Show trigger input'.

Three identical wires, no numeral anywhere. n8n runs the branch whose tile sits highest, leftmost breaking ties — so dragging `close` above `open` crushes the gripper on nothing without changing a single connection.
No trigger box and no numbers: an outlet fires its cords right-to-left, so `validate` runs first only because its box sits further right. Nudge it left and the patch silently reorders.
Not a single wire on the board. The order is nothing but the small grey numeral sitting against each state, assigned from where the state was drawn and silently renumbered when you move one.

all three fire after the loop

spec.cap: This is the one bucket that gets Python right: the Get node reads the name when the delegate FIRES, long after the loop wrote it last — the absent wire IS the closure cell.
LabVIEW has no way to read k that is not a wire, so the hidden input becomes a visible stub — and make_scaler stops existing: there is one VI taking two arguments.
Python wrote `def local()` with an empty parameter list; the capsule shows two grips, so the drawing contradicts the signature and the signature is the one that was lying.

wires.t: list — drawn as a double line

spec.cap: Promotion answers a different question: i arrives on the port the moment it exists, so the board can only say 0, 1, 2 — Python's 2, 2, 2 needs a cell these boards do not have.
One cable enters the hull from outside and that is the entire capture — Closure Input declares p and only p, so the crossing is the visual difference between an argument and a capture.
Closure Input carries no rows because local() takes no arguments — yet two cables cross the hull, so the zone's real arity is two and only the hull crossing says so.

nodes.t: A socket holds exactly one cable and a cable has one source forever, so there is no cell to re-read. The hull can snapshot a value; nothing can make that value change afterwards, and there is no list-of-closures socket to hold three of them.

spec.cap: The zone captures by wire, and a wire is not a variable — late binding needs a name that can be written twice, which is the one thing this vocabulary refuses to draw.

nodes.t: Undrawable. A parameter row holds text: the [] typed into it is re-parsed into a fresh list every run, so nothing survives between calls. The nearest shape is Node-RED flow context or n8n static data — a named store, a different construct entirely.

spec.cap: A panel row has no identity to share, so the definition can hand out a value but never the same object twice.

Three Python statements, one unbroken wire: a LabVIEW wire has exactly one source forever, so rebinding the name `bundle` twice cannot be drawn at all — the name is simply the wire running through both nodes.

The dots of the fluent chain are the noodle itself — and Set Material emits NEW geometry rather than editing the old, so the 'mutation chain' is a copy chain that draws exactly like board 1; `tex` never becomes a node, it is a dropdown on the node face.

Python reads inside-out, the canvas reads left-to-right: the innermost call is the leftmost node — and both Set rows could be folded into ONE change dialog (or one Simulink Bus Assignment, one n8n Edit Fields tile), at which point the chain vanishes from the canvas entirely.

Only the first `bundle =` is a SET node; the other two re-assignments are drawn nowhere, because the object goes in on Target and nothing comes out — the white wire is the sole evidence that the mesh was added before the texture.

The `.` between the two method calls IS the white control edge — and because nothing carries the receiver forward, the same green data wire has to be run to a second Target port, so the fluent chain is drawn twice over: once as control, once as data.

nodes.t: Unreal — a Target-pin call with no Return Value cannot sit inside another call's pin, so `with_texture(with_mesh(…))` has to be redrawn as board 1's exec line.
Unity — the same, and the escape is to leave: give the method a return value and the white wire disappears, and the board becomes the cable in 'Object in left, object out right'.

spec.cap: The only spelling in the whole facet a mechanism cannot draw — and the workaround is not a different node, it is a different mechanism.

Python adds the mesh first; the patch must load the texture first — the cold right inlet has to be set before the hot left inlet fires — so the drawing runs the source order backwards, and the right outlet of `t b b` is the only thing that says so.

Both cords leave one outlet and Max fires them right-to-left by where their boxes sit, so the fluent chain's order is a property of screen position: drag `mesh` to the right of `tex` and the bundle comes out wrong — which is exactly why board 1's trigger exists.

Nesting is the one spelling Max draws as a chain of cords — the inner call must hand something back for the outer one to take — and it reads bottom-up, innermost box at the top; the arguments are typed into the box text, so no cord shows them at all.
